items.prompt: Tell me about yourself.
items.framing: The opener tests whether you can present a coherent, self-aware story in about two minutes. The panel uses it to pick threads for follow-up, so whatever you mention becomes the agenda for the next twenty minutes.
structure: Open with one line on who you are today (education or role), not your birth date or full family tree
Walk through two or three defining choices - academics, work or activities - and what each taught you
Pick one concrete achievement or episode with a specific detail that makes you memorable
Close by linking where you are now to why an MBA is the logical next step, in one sentence
avoid: Reciting your CV line by line - the panel already has it
Dropping topics you cannot defend under follow-up questions
Running past two to three minutes

items.prompt: Introduce yourself, but tell us something that is not on your CV.
items.framing: The panel wants the person behind the paperwork: values, curiosity and how you spend your time when no one is grading you. It also checks whether you can think on your feet when the rehearsed script is ruled out.
structure: Acknowledge the ask briefly and skip the résumé summary entirely
Share one or two genuine traits, habits or experiences - a responsibility at home, a long-running interest, a turning point
Back each with a short, specific example rather than an adjective
Tie it lightly to how it shapes the way you work or learn
avoid: Repeating CV facts in different words
Inventing an exotic hobby you cannot discuss in depth

items.prompt: Describe yourself in three words.
items.framing: A compression test: can you choose precise words and prove them? The panel checks self-awareness and whether others would agree with your self-image.
structure: Choose three distinct qualities that do not overlap (for example one about work style, one about people, one about mindset)
Give a one-line proof for each from your own life
Optionally mention how a friend or manager would describe you, if it matches
avoid: Generic words like hardworking, honest, dedicated with no evidence
Picking words that contradict your CV or the way you are answering

items.prompt: Why do you want to do an MBA?
items.framing: The core motivation question. The panel looks for a reason rooted in your experience, a clear gap the MBA fills, and evidence that you have thought beyond salary and brand.
structure: Start from a concrete moment in your academics or work where you saw the limits of your current skills
Name the specific capabilities you want - for example financial judgement, people management, strategy - and why they matter for your goal
Explain why a structured MBA, rather than learning on the job, is the efficient way to build them
Connect to your short-term goal so the answer feels like a plan, not a wish
avoid: Leading with salary, placements or peer pressure
Vague lines like 'to get holistic development' or 'managerial exposure'
A reason that applies equally to every candidate in the room

items.prompt: Why an MBA now? Why not after a few more years?
items.framing: Timing questions test whether you have a reason for this moment - readiness, a career inflection point, or learning saturation - and whether you have weighed the trade-off of waiting.
structure: State what has changed recently that makes now the right time (role ceiling, clarity of goal, a skill gap you keep hitting)
Show what you have already gained from your current stage and what more years would add only marginally
Acknowledge the merit of waiting, then explain why it does not outweigh starting now for your goal
Keep the tone confident, not defensive
avoid: Saying 'the earlier the better' with no personal reasoning
Criticising people who do an MBA later

items.prompt: Why our institute? What do you know about us?
items.framing: The panel checks whether you researched the institute or are simply applying everywhere. Specific, accurate, personally relevant reasons signal genuine fit; generic praise signals the opposite.
structure: Before the interview, read the institute's own website: curriculum structure, electives, pedagogy, clubs, centres, location and recent student initiatives
Pick two or three features that connect directly to your goals or background and name them precisely
Explain how you would use each one - a course, a club you would join, an industry cluster near the campus
Close with what you would add to the community, so fit runs both ways
avoid: Quoting rankings or placement figures as your main reason
Stating facts you are not sure of - an error here hurts more than saying less
Praise that could be pasted for any college

items.prompt: Which other institutes have you applied to or received calls from?
items.framing: An honesty and consistency check. The panel wants a truthful answer and to see that your choices follow a logic, not desperation.
structure: Answer truthfully and briefly; there is nothing wrong with having other calls
Mention the common thread in your choices (programme type, specialisation strength, location) if there is one
Reaffirm why this institute fits you, without sounding as if you are bargaining
avoid: Lying or hiding calls
Belittling other institutes
Saying you would join anywhere that admits you

items.prompt: What is your short-term goal after the MBA?
items.framing: The panel checks clarity and realism: a specific role, function and type of organisation that a fresh MBA with your background can credibly reach.
structure: Name a role and function (for example product management, corporate finance, sales leadership) and the kind of organisation
Explain why your background plus the MBA makes you a credible candidate for it
Mention one or two skills you will deliberately build during the programme to get there
Keep a plausible alternative in mind in case the panel probes
avoid: Saying 'I am open to anything' or 'I will decide after the first year'
Aiming at a role that is unrealistic straight out of an MBA, such as CEO

items.prompt: Where do you see yourself in ten years?
items.framing: Long-term goals test direction and values more than precise titles. The panel wants a sensible arc from your short-term goal and some sense of the impact you want to have.
structure: Describe the kind of responsibility or impact you want, not just a designation
Show the logical path from your short-term goal to this destination
Mention a value or motivation behind it - building something, leading teams, solving a problem you care about
Stay flexible: acknowledge that the route may change while the direction holds
avoid: Grandiose claims you cannot connect to anything you have done
Goals that contradict your short-term plan

items.prompt: What are your key strengths?
items.framing: Self-awareness backed by evidence. The panel will often test the claimed strength later in the interview, so it must be real and relevant to management.
structure: Pick two strengths that are relevant to a manager's job
Prove each with a specific situation, what you did and the result
Show how each strength will help you in the MBA or your target role
avoid: Listing many adjectives with no examples
Claiming a strength your answers in the room contradict, such as communication while rambling

items.prompt: What is your biggest weakness?
items.framing: A test of honesty and growth. The panel wants a real weakness, evidence that you understand its impact, and concrete steps you are taking about it.
structure: Name a genuine, work-relevant weakness that is not a core requirement of your target role
Give a brief example of when it affected you or a team
Describe the specific actions you are taking and any progress so far
Keep it matter-of-fact - neither dramatic nor dismissive
avoid: Disguised strengths like 'I am a perfectionist' or 'I work too hard'
A weakness that disqualifies you for your stated goal
Having no improvement plan

items.prompt: Tell us about your hometown.
items.framing: Checks your awareness of your surroundings: economy, culture, challenges and opportunities. Interviewers often follow up with what you would do to develop it, so think like a manager, not a tourist guide.
structure: Give a quick picture: where it is, what it is known for and what drives its economy
Mention one or two challenges it faces and why they persist
Suggest one realistic opportunity or idea a business or administrator could pursue there
Be ready for questions on local industries, history or notable places
avoid: Only listing monuments and food
Quoting numbers you are not sure of
Having no view on its problems or potential

items.prompt: Tell us about your family. How have they influenced you?
items.framing: The panel is not judging your family; it is looking for values, influences and how your upbringing shaped your choices.
structure: Briefly describe your family and what they do, without excessive detail
Pick one or two values or habits you absorbed and give an example of each
Link those values to how you work, study or make decisions today
avoid: A long list of relatives' designations
Using family status to impress
Oversharing private matters you are uncomfortable discussing

items.prompt: There is a gap in your education or career. What did you do during that time?
items.framing: Gaps are not disqualifying; unexplained or poorly used ones raise doubts. The panel wants honesty, ownership and evidence of productive use of time.
structure: State the reason plainly and honestly - exam preparation, health, family responsibility, a venture, or a career rethink
Describe what you did during the period: learning, projects, responsibilities, part-time work
Share what you learned about yourself and how it informs your decision now
Show that the gap is behind you and you are ready for an intense programme
avoid: Being defensive or apologetic
Inventing activities you cannot discuss in detail
Blaming circumstances without any ownership

items.prompt: This is not your first attempt at CAT. Why should we read that positively?
items.framing: The panel checks persistence, reflection and whether you improved meaningfully between attempts rather than simply repeating.
structure: Acknowledge the earlier attempt(s) without excuses
Explain what you diagnosed as the gap and what you changed in your approach
Mention what else you did in the meantime - work, learning, responsibilities
Frame it as evidence of commitment to a clear goal
avoid: Blaming the exam, luck or difficulty level
Sounding as if the MBA is an obsession with no fallback thinking

items.prompt: What will you contribute to your batch and the institute?
items.framing: MBA learning is heavily peer-driven. The panel wants to know what specific experience, skill or energy you bring to classrooms, clubs and group work.
structure: Identify one or two things that are genuinely distinctive about you - domain knowledge, a skill, a perspective, an activity
Give a concrete example of how you have contributed this in a past group
Translate it into a specific contribution: a club, a peer-learning effort, case discussions, events
avoid: Generic promises like 'I will be a good team player'
Claiming you will start many clubs without evidence of past initiative

items.prompt: What will you do if you do not get admitted this year?
items.framing: Tests maturity and resilience. The panel wants a calm, realistic plan that shows you are committed to your goal but not paralysed by one outcome.
structure: Say calmly that you would reflect on feedback and strengthen your profile
Describe concrete steps: continue or deepen your work, build a specific skill, reattempt with a better strategy
Reaffirm that your long-term goal remains, regardless of the timeline
avoid: Saying you have not thought about it
Sounding desperate or pleading
A plan B that contradicts your stated reasons for an MBA

items.prompt: Which specialisation do you plan to take and why?
items.framing: Checks whether your stated goals and your understanding of the curriculum line up, and whether you know what the specialisation actually involves.
structure: Name the specialisation, or the two you are weighing, honestly
Connect it to your background and short-term goal
Show you understand what the work involves day to day, not just the label
If undecided, say how you will use the first year to decide
avoid: Picking a specialisation because it pays well, with no other reason
Being unable to describe a single subject or role within it

items.prompt: Who is your role model and why?
items.framing: The panel learns about your values through whom you admire. It is less about the person and more about the qualities you want to emulate and how you act on them.
structure: Choose someone you genuinely know about - it can be a public figure or someone in your own life
Name the specific qualities you admire, with an incident or decision that shows them
Explain how you try to apply those qualities in your own life
avoid: Choosing a famous name you cannot discuss in depth
Listing achievements without saying what you learned

items.prompt: What has been your proudest achievement so far?
items.framing: Reveals what you value and how you define success. The panel looks at the scale of the challenge, your specific role and what it says about you.
structure: Pick an achievement where your own contribution was decisive
Set the context and the difficulty briefly
Explain what you did and the result, using specifics rather than superlatives
Share why it matters to you personally
avoid: Choosing something where your role was minor
Picking a very old school-level achievement when recent ones exist

items.prompt: Why should we select you over the other candidates?
items.framing: A pitch question. The panel wants a confident, evidence-based summary of your fit, without arrogance or putting others down.
structure: Summarise two or three qualities or experiences that make you a strong fit for the programme
Back each with a quick proof point the panel has already heard or can verify
Connect them to what you will do with the MBA and add to the class
End with a short, sincere statement of commitment
avoid: Comparing yourself to or criticising other candidates
Saying 'I deserve it' without evidence

items.prompt: Tell us about a time you failed and what you learned.
items.framing: Tests ownership, reflection and resilience. The panel cares far more about what you did next than about the failure itself.
structure: Choose a real failure with genuine stakes, not a trivial one
Describe the situation and your role honestly, owning your part
Explain what you learned and what you changed
Give evidence that the change worked in a later situation
avoid: Choosing a fake failure that is really a success
Blaming others or circumstances
Stopping at the failure with no learning

items.prompt: Tell us about a difficult decision you made and how you made it.
items.framing: Assesses judgement and values: how you weigh options, handle uncertainty and live with trade-offs.
structure: Set up the decision and why it was genuinely hard - competing goals, people or values
Explain the options you considered and the criteria you used
State what you chose and what you gave up
Reflect on the outcome and whether you would decide the same way again
avoid: Picking a decision with an obvious right answer
Claiming you had no doubts at all

items.prompt: What is the most useful feedback you have received?
items.framing: Checks coachability. The panel wants to see that you can hear criticism, accept it and change.
structure: Describe the feedback and who gave it, briefly
Be honest about your initial reaction
Explain what you changed as a result and the effect it had
avoid: Choosing praise disguised as feedback
Sounding as if the feedback was unfair

items.prompt: Do you have any questions for us?
items.framing: The closing question still counts. A thoughtful question shows genuine interest and research; a weak one, or a question about placements alone, can undo good work.
structure: Prepare one or two questions that cannot be answered from the institute's website
Ask about something tied to your goals - how students typically use a particular aspect of the programme, or advice for someone with your background
Listen to the answer and thank the panel briefly
avoid: Asking about salaries or placements first
Asking something easily found online
Asking about your result or how you did

items.prompt: Explain your final-year project as if I am not an engineer.
items.framing: Tests whether you understand your own work deeply enough to simplify it, and whether you can communicate with non-technical stakeholders - a core managerial skill.
structure: Start with the problem the project solves and who would care, in everyday language
Use one analogy to explain how your solution works
Describe your personal role and one hard decision or obstacle
End with the result, its limitations and a possible real-world use
avoid: Diving into jargon and equations
Overstating the project's impact or novelty
Being unable to explain the parts your teammates did

items.prompt: Why did you choose engineering, and why move to management now?
items.framing: The panel wants a coherent narrative rather than an admission that both choices were defaults. Moving on is fine if you can show what engineering gave you and what it cannot.
structure: Be honest about why you chose engineering, even if it was partly a default
Name what engineering gave you - analytical thinking, structured problem-solving, comfort with data
Explain the point where you became interested in the business side of technical work
Show how the MBA builds on, rather than discards, your engineering background
avoid: Saying you never liked engineering, which raises doubts about your commitment to an MBA too
'Everyone in my batch is doing it'

items.prompt: Explain one fundamental concept from your branch that you consider important.
items.framing: A depth check. The panel wants to see that you retained the fundamentals of four years of study and can explain them clearly and accurately.
structure: Pick a concept you understand thoroughly rather than an impressive one you only recall partially
Define it simply, then explain why it matters with a practical example
Connect it to a product, system or industry where it is used
Be ready for one or two levels of follow-up questions
avoid: Choosing a topic you studied only for an exam and have forgotten
Mixing up definitions under pressure - say what you are unsure of

items.prompt: How is technology from your field changing the way businesses operate?
items.framing: Assesses your ability to connect technical knowledge with business outcomes - cost, speed, quality, new business models and risks.
structure: Pick one or two technologies relevant to your branch
Explain plainly what they do differently from older approaches
Describe the business effect: costs, customer experience, new products, or changes to jobs and skills
Mention a risk or limitation for balance
avoid: Listing buzzwords with no explanation
Quoting statistics or company claims you cannot verify

items.prompt: Which was your favourite subject in engineering, and which did you find hardest?
items.framing: The panel will probe whichever subject you name, so it checks honesty and depth. How you dealt with the hard subject reveals your learning approach.
structure: Name a favourite subject you can genuinely discuss in some depth and say why it interested you
Name a difficult subject honestly
Explain how you approached the difficulty and what you learned about learning
avoid: Naming a favourite subject you cannot answer basic questions on
Saying nothing was difficult

items.prompt: Your academic scores are average. What happened?
items.framing: Tests ownership and maturity. The panel wants an honest explanation without excuses and evidence that you can perform when it matters.
structure: Acknowledge the scores directly without becoming defensive
Give an honest reason in one or two sentences - where your energy went or what you misjudged
Point to evidence of capability elsewhere: projects, work, test scores, activities
State what you have changed in how you learn
avoid: Blaming professors, the university or the system
Over-explaining for minutes

items.prompt: What can an engineer bring to management that others cannot?
items.framing: Checks how you see your own background as an asset, and whether you can do so without dismissing other backgrounds.
structure: Name two or three transferable strengths such as structured problem-solving, quantitative comfort, process thinking
Give a short example of each from your experience
Acknowledge what engineers often need to learn, such as people skills or market perspective
Say how a diverse class helps you learn exactly that
avoid: Claiming engineers are better managers
Ignoring your own blind spots

items.prompt: Give an example of a trade-off that engineers routinely make, and relate it to a business decision.
items.framing: Tests applied thinking: engineering is about constraints and trade-offs, and so is management. The panel wants you to draw the parallel clearly.
structure: Describe a common trade-off in your field, such as cost versus durability, speed versus accuracy, or performance versus power
Explain how engineers decide - requirements, constraints, testing
Map it to an equivalent business decision such as price versus volume or speed to market versus quality
Draw out the shared principle
avoid: Getting the technical trade-off wrong
A forced analogy that does not hold

items.prompt: Tell us about working in a team on an engineering project. What was your role?
items.framing: The panel probes your real contribution and how you handled the usual problems of group work - uneven effort, disagreement, deadlines.
structure: Briefly describe the project, team size and objective
State your specific responsibilities clearly
Describe one team problem and how you helped resolve it
Mention the outcome and what you would do differently
avoid: Saying 'we' throughout so your role is invisible
Criticising teammates

items.prompt: Name an industry that relies heavily on your branch of engineering and describe one challenge it faces.
items.framing: Checks industry awareness and whether you think beyond the textbook about how your discipline creates value.
structure: Pick an industry where your branch is clearly central
Explain how your discipline is used in its products or operations
Describe one lasting challenge - cost pressure, safety, sustainability, skills, supply chains
Suggest how better management or technology could help address it
avoid: Citing specific figures or company facts you are unsure of
Describing the industry only at a superficial level

items.prompt: Why an MBA after your commerce degree? Isn't it repetition?
items.framing: Tests whether you understand how an MBA differs from a commerce degree - application, decision-making, leadership and integration across functions - and whether you have a real reason.
structure: Acknowledge the overlap honestly - some concepts will be familiar
Explain the difference: a commerce degree builds concepts, an MBA applies them to decisions through cases, projects and peer learning
Name the specific gaps you want to fill, such as strategy, analytics, leadership or a specialisation
Show how your commerce foundation lets you go deeper faster
avoid: Saying the MBA is the natural next step with no reason
Dismissing your commerce degree as useless

items.prompt: What is depreciation, and why do businesses charge it?
items.framing: A fundamentals check. The panel wants conceptual clarity - matching the cost of an asset to the periods it helps earn revenue - not memorised formulas.
structure: Define it simply: spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life
Explain the reason: matching expense with the revenue the asset helps generate, so profits are not distorted
Note that it is a non-cash expense and mention common methods (such as straight-line and written-down value) at a high level
Mention its effect on reported profit and on tax, and be ready for an example
avoid: Calling depreciation a cash outflow
Reciting formulas without the intuition

items.prompt: Explain working capital and why a profitable company can still run out of cash.
items.framing: Tests understanding of the difference between profit and cash, which is central to finance and management.
structure: Define working capital simply as current assets minus current liabilities - the funds tied up in day-to-day operations
Explain the cycle: buying inventory, selling on credit, waiting to collect, paying suppliers
Show how a profitable firm can still face a cash crunch if collections are slow or inventory piles up
Mention levers to manage it: collection, inventory and supplier terms
avoid: Equating profit with cash
Giving only a formula with no explanation

items.prompt: Explain an accounting principle you consider fundamental and why it matters.
items.framing: Checks conceptual depth and whether you can connect rules to their purpose - reliable, comparable financial information.
structure: Pick a principle you know well, such as accrual, matching, consistency, prudence or going concern
Define it in plain language
Give a simple example of how it changes what appears in the accounts
Explain what would go wrong for users of financial statements without it
avoid: Confusing principles with each other
Using jargon you cannot explain

items.prompt: How would you judge a company's health from its financial statements?
items.framing: Tests whether you can read the three statements together and think like an analyst rather than a bookkeeper.
structure: Explain what each statement shows: performance (profit and loss), position (balance sheet), cash movement (cash flow)
Mention the dimensions you would check: profitability, liquidity, leverage and efficiency, with an example ratio for each
Stress comparing over time and against peers rather than reading a single number
Note that the notes and qualitative factors also matter
avoid: Relying on a single ratio
Mixing up which statement shows what

items.prompt: You attempted CA (or another professional course). Why did you move away from it?
items.framing: The panel checks whether the switch is a considered choice or an escape, and what you carried forward from that preparation.
structure: Explain honestly where you reached and what led you to rethink
Show what that preparation gave you - technical depth, discipline, exam resilience
Explain why management fits your goals better than continuing
Keep it forward-looking, without disparaging the course
avoid: Sounding as if you are running from failure
Blaming the difficulty of the exams

items.prompt: Explain the difference between direct and indirect taxes, with an example of each.
items.framing: A basic economic literacy check. The panel looks for clear concepts and an awareness of how taxes affect consumers and businesses.
structure: Define direct taxes as levied on income or wealth and paid by the person taxed
Define indirect taxes as levied on goods and services and ultimately borne by the consumer
Give a common example of each
Mention one business implication, such as pricing or compliance
avoid: Quoting specific tax rates that may be out of date
Mixing up who bears the tax

items.prompt: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs, and why does it matter for a business?
items.framing: Tests understanding of cost behaviour, which drives pricing, break-even and scaling decisions.
structure: Define each simply with an everyday business example
Explain contribution: price minus variable cost per unit, which covers fixed costs
Link to break-even and to why high fixed-cost businesses push for volume
Mention that some costs are semi-variable and the classification depends on time frame
avoid: Treating all costs as fixed in the short run
Giving a definition with no application

items.prompt: How has your commerce education helped you understand the businesses around you?
items.framing: Checks whether you can apply classroom learning to the real world - a local shop, a family business or an employer.
structure: Pick a business you know well
Describe how concepts such as margins, working capital, credit or pricing show up in its operations
Share an insight or improvement you noticed using those concepts
avoid: Staying purely theoretical
Choosing a large company you know only from headlines

items.prompt: What role do banks play in an economy?
items.framing: A broad fundamentals question to test conceptual clarity on intermediation, credit and money - topics commerce graduates are expected to handle.
structure: Explain intermediation: pooling savings and lending to borrowers
Mention credit creation, payments and risk management
Note the role of the central bank in regulating and supporting the system, in general terms
Give one example of how bank health affects businesses
avoid: Quoting specific policy rates or recent figures
Confusing commercial banks with the central bank

items.prompt: How is your arts or humanities major relevant to management?
items.framing: The panel tests whether you see your background as an asset. Management is about people, societies, communication and judgement, and the humanities train exactly these.
structure: Name your major and its core concerns in one line
Identify two or three transferable skills - understanding people, critical reading, writing, argument, cultural awareness
Give an example of how one of these applies to a business situation
Acknowledge the quantitative skills you are building and how
avoid: Being apologetic about your background
Ignoring the quantitative demands of an MBA

items.prompt: Tell us about a thinker or an idea from your field that has influenced you.
items.framing: Checks intellectual engagement and depth. The panel will likely probe, so pick an idea you truly understand and can relate to the real world.
structure: Choose an idea or thinker you have actually studied and can discuss
Explain the core idea in simple terms
Say why it influenced you, with an example
Relate it to organisations, leadership or society today
avoid: Name-dropping a famous thinker you only know superficially
Misrepresenting the idea

items.prompt: What research methods did you learn in your course, and how might they be useful in business?
items.framing: Tests whether you understand evidence - how to ask questions, gather data and judge conclusions - and can connect that to decisions in business.
structure: Name the methods you used, such as surveys, interviews, archival work, fieldwork or textual analysis
Explain the strengths and limitations of one method you used
Connect it to a business use such as customer research, policy analysis or market understanding
Mention an example from your own coursework if possible
avoid: Claiming methods you did not use
Treating qualitative evidence as weaker by default, or vice versa

items.prompt: Why did you choose arts, and why management now?
items.framing: The panel wants a coherent story connecting your interests to your new direction, not an apology for your earlier choice.
structure: Explain what drew you to your subject
Describe what made you interested in how organisations work - an internship, a project, a responsibility
Show how the MBA builds on your perspective rather than replacing it
Connect to a specific goal
avoid: Saying arts was a fallback with no further reflection
Abandoning your subject's value entirely

items.prompt: An MBA is quantitative. How will you cope coming from an arts background?
items.framing: A readiness check. The panel wants honesty and evidence that you can handle quantitative coursework.
structure: Acknowledge the gap honestly
Point to evidence: your aptitude test performance, any statistics or economics courses, self-learning
Describe a concrete preparation plan before and during the programme
Mention how you would use peers and resources
avoid: Claiming there is no gap
Saying you will avoid quantitative electives

items.prompt: How does understanding society or culture help a business succeed?
items.framing: Tests your ability to link humanities insight to markets - consumer behaviour, communication, ethics and diverse workforces.
structure: Explain that customers and employees are shaped by culture, language and social context
Give an example of how that understanding shapes a product, message or workplace
Mention a risk of ignoring it, such as a misjudged campaign or a poor policy
Tie it back to your own studies
avoid: Citing specific corporate controversies you are unsure of
Staying abstract with no example

items.prompt: How have writing and argument skills from your degree helped you?
items.framing: Communication is central to management. The panel checks whether you can show these skills rather than simply claim them.
structure: Give an example of writing or argument you did - a dissertation, debate, publication or presentation
Explain how you structure an argument: claim, evidence, counter-view, conclusion
Connect it to managerial tasks such as reports, persuasion and negotiation
avoid: Rambling while claiming strong communication
Generic claims with no example

items.prompt: How is your subject relevant to the world today?
items.framing: Checks whether you see your discipline as alive and applied. The panel wants a thoughtful link to contemporary questions without depending on specific news.
structure: Pick a lasting question your subject helps understand - identity, governance, inequality, media, behaviour
Explain how your discipline approaches it
Connect it to organisations or policy
Offer your own view
avoid: Relying on a single news item you cannot discuss in depth
Treating your subject as purely historical

items.prompt: Tell us about a significant paper or dissertation you wrote.
items.framing: Tests depth, independent thinking and your ability to explain your own research.
structure: State the question you investigated and why it interested you
Explain your approach and sources
Summarise your main finding and its limitations
Say what the experience taught you about inquiry
avoid: Being unable to explain your own conclusions
Overclaiming originality

items.prompt: Pick a concept from your major and explain how a manager could use it.
items.framing: Tests applied thinking: can you translate an idea from your discipline into a practical managerial tool?
structure: Choose a concept you know well, for example from psychology, economics, sociology or literature
Define it simply
Show how a manager could apply it - motivating a team, designing an incentive, understanding customers
Mention a limitation
avoid: Choosing a concept you cannot explain accurately
Forcing an application that does not hold

items.prompt: How can the scientific method help in business decision-making?
items.framing: Tests whether you can transfer a disciplined way of thinking - hypotheses, testing, evidence - to managerial problems.
structure: Outline the method briefly: observe, hypothesise, test, analyse, revise
Map it to a business example such as testing a new price, a product feature or a process change
Discuss the role of controls, sample size and bias in avoiding wrong conclusions
Note where business differs - time pressure, incomplete data, human factors
avoid: Getting basic steps of the method wrong
Implying every business decision can be run as a controlled experiment

items.prompt: How is your specialisation applied in industry?
items.framing: Checks whether you know where your subject creates value and can connect science to business.
structure: Name your specialisation and its core focus
Describe two or three industries or products that depend on it
Explain the business challenge in one of them - cost, regulation, scale-up, research timelines
Show where management skills matter in that chain
avoid: Citing specific company facts or figures you are unsure of
Listing industries without explaining the link

items.prompt: Tell us about your lab work. What did it teach you about working in a team?
items.framing: Tests teamwork, rigour and patience. Lab work involves shared equipment, protocols, failed experiments and careful documentation.
structure: Describe a lab project or practical briefly and your role in it
Share a team challenge - coordination, a failed experiment, a disagreement over method
Explain how you handled it
Connect the habits you built (documentation, precision, patience) to management
avoid: Describing only technical steps with no reflection
Taking credit for others' work

items.prompt: Why move from science to management?
items.framing: The panel looks for a coherent motive and checks you are not abandoning science without reflection.
structure: Explain what drew you to science and what you valued in it
Describe the moment you became interested in how science reaches people - commercialisation, policy, operations
Show how an MBA helps you work at that intersection
Connect to a specific goal
avoid: Saying you could not find a job in science
Dismissing your degree

items.prompt: Explain a core concept from your subject in simple terms.
items.framing: A depth and communication check. The panel wants accuracy plus clarity for a non-specialist audience.
structure: Pick a concept you know thoroughly
Explain it with an everyday analogy
Mention an application in daily life or industry
Be ready for follow-up and admit honestly where your knowledge ends
avoid: Choosing something you cannot explain accurately
Using heavy jargon

items.prompt: How do you know when data supports a conclusion and when it does not?
items.framing: Tests statistical thinking that science students should have and managers need: correlation versus causation, sample size, bias and uncertainty.
structure: Mention checks: sample size and representativeness, controls, measurement quality
Explain correlation versus causation with a simple example
Discuss uncertainty and the value of replication
Relate to a business setting such as interpreting a survey or a sales trend
avoid: Confusing correlation with causation in your own example
Being overconfident about any single result

items.prompt: Why do many scientific discoveries take a long time to reach the market?
items.framing: Tests understanding of the journey from lab to product - development, testing, regulation, manufacturing and business viability.
structure: Describe the stages broadly: research, development, testing, approval where required, scale-up, launch
Explain the challenges at each - cost, safety, reproducibility, manufacturing at scale
Mention the business side: funding, market fit, pricing
Suggest where better management can shorten the journey
avoid: Claiming specific timelines or figures as fact
Ignoring the role of safety and regulation

items.prompt: What ethical issues do you see in your field of science?
items.framing: Assesses awareness of responsibility and ability to reason about trade-offs - relevant to future managers in regulated or sensitive industries.
structure: Name one or two genuine ethical concerns in your field, such as data, safety, environment or consent
Explain the competing interests involved
Offer a balanced view on how to handle them
Link to how organisations should govern such issues
avoid: Taking an extreme position without considering the other side
Inventing specific incidents

items.prompt: Describe an experiment or project that did not work. What did you do?
items.framing: Tests resilience and problem-solving. Science involves frequent failure; the panel wants your debugging process and attitude.
structure: Describe the experiment and the expected result
Explain what went wrong and how you diagnosed it
Describe the changes you made and the result
Draw a lesson that applies beyond the lab
avoid: Blaming equipment or teammates
Having no systematic diagnosis

items.prompt: What advantage does a science background give you in an MBA?
items.framing: Checks self-awareness about transferable strengths, and humility about gaps.
structure: Name two strengths such as quantitative comfort, rigour, hypothesis-driven thinking
Give an example of each
Acknowledge a gap, such as business vocabulary or commercial exposure, and how you are closing it
avoid: Claiming superiority over other backgrounds
Listing strengths without evidence

items.prompt: Describe your current role and a typical day at work.
items.framing: The panel checks whether you understand your role in the context of the organisation and can describe it clearly to outsiders.
structure: Start with the organisation and your team's purpose in one line
Describe your key responsibilities and who you work with
Walk through a typical day or week briefly
Mention how your output is measured and how it affects the business
avoid: Heavy internal jargon or acronyms
Overstating your seniority or scope

items.prompt: What is your biggest achievement at work?
items.framing: Looks for impact and ownership. The panel wants your specific contribution, the challenge involved and a measurable or observable result.
structure: Set the context and the problem briefly
Explain what you specifically did, including any initiative beyond your role
Describe the outcome in concrete terms - time saved, quality improved, customers helped - without inventing numbers
Mention what you learned
avoid: Taking credit for team results without clarifying your role
Claiming exaggerated figures

items.prompt: Tell us about a mistake you made at work.
items.framing: Tests ownership and maturity. The panel wants to see that you can admit errors, fix them and prevent them in future.
structure: Describe the mistake honestly and its impact
Explain how you took responsibility and handled the immediate situation
Describe what you changed to prevent a repeat
Keep the tone reflective, not defensive
avoid: Picking a trivial or fake mistake
Blaming others

items.prompt: Tell us about a disagreement with your manager. How did you handle it?
items.framing: Tests professionalism, communication and judgement - can you disagree respectfully and still deliver?
structure: Describe the disagreement and why it mattered
Explain how you raised your view - with data, privately, respectfully
Describe the outcome, including if you were overruled
Reflect on what you learned about working with authority
avoid: Portraying your manager as incompetent
A story where you simply gave in with no reasoning

items.prompt: Describe a conflict with a colleague and how it was resolved.
items.framing: Assesses interpersonal skills and emotional maturity, which matter in group-heavy MBA programmes and in management.
structure: Set the context and the source of conflict
Explain how you tried to understand the other person's view
Describe the steps you took to resolve it
Mention the result and the relationship afterwards
avoid: Making yourself the hero and the colleague the villain
Saying you have never had a conflict

items.prompt: Why do you want to leave your job?
items.framing: The panel checks whether you are moving towards something or simply escaping. A forward-looking, respectful answer works best.
structure: Acknowledge what you have gained from your job
Explain the limit you have reached in learning or scope
Connect the move to your goals and the MBA
Stay positive about your employer
avoid: Complaining about pay, your boss or the company
Sounding as if you have not given the job a fair chance

items.prompt: How does your work add value to your company?
items.framing: Tests business understanding: can you trace your daily output to revenue, cost, quality, risk or customers?
structure: Describe your main output
Trace how it affects the business - customers served, costs reduced, risks managed, revenue enabled
Give one concrete example
Suggest one way your role could add more value
avoid: Describing tasks without impact
Claiming responsibility for company-level results

items.prompt: You have no work experience. Why should we not wait for you to gain some?
items.framing: The panel wants to know whether you have the clarity and maturity to benefit from an MBA without work experience, and what you have done instead.
structure: Acknowledge the value of work experience honestly
Show the clarity you already have about your goals and why the MBA fits now
Point to substitutes: internships, projects, leadership roles, responsibilities
Explain how you will make up for it - learning from experienced peers, live projects, summer internship
avoid: Claiming work experience does not matter
Having no examples of real-world exposure

items.prompt: Tell us about your internship. What did you learn?
items.framing: For freshers this replaces the work discussion. The panel probes your actual contribution and what you learned about organisations.
structure: Describe the organisation, your team and your project
Explain your specific contribution and the outcome
Share one insight about how the business works
Mention how it shaped your goals
avoid: Describing only what the company does
Overstating your role in the project

items.prompt: Tell us about a time you led without formal authority.
items.framing: Leadership through influence is central to management. The panel looks for initiative, persuasion and results.
structure: Describe the situation and why leadership was needed
Explain how you influenced others - building credibility, finding common goals, taking the first step
Describe the outcome
Reflect on what you learned about influence
avoid: Describing a situation where you had a title
Implying you forced others to comply

items.prompt: What would your manager say are your strengths and areas of improvement?
items.framing: Tests self-awareness and consistency with what you have said elsewhere. Answers often match reference views or appraisals.
structure: State one or two strengths your manager would cite, with an example
State one area of improvement honestly
Mention what you are doing about it
avoid: Only listing strengths
Contradicting what you said in other answers

items.prompt: What are the major challenges facing your industry?
items.framing: Checks whether you see beyond your desk to the competitive and economic forces shaping your sector.
structure: Name two or three lasting challenges - competition, technology, regulation, talent, costs
Explain how each affects companies like yours
Describe how your organisation or industry is responding in general terms
Give your own view
avoid: Quoting news or figures you cannot back up
Being unaware of anything outside your role

items.prompt: How will your work experience help you in the MBA classroom?
items.framing: The panel wants to know what you bring to case discussions and group work.
structure: Identify the functional and industry knowledge you have
Give an example of a situation you could bring into discussions
Mention skills such as deadlines, client handling or teamwork
Say what you hope to learn from peers with other experience
avoid: Sounding as if you already know everything
Generic claims

items.prompt: Your goal is in a different function from your current work. Is that not a waste of your experience?
items.framing: Tests whether your career switch is thought through and whether you see the transferable value in your experience.
structure: Acknowledge the switch directly
Show which skills and insights from your work transfer to the new function
Explain why the new function suits you better, with evidence
Describe how the MBA bridges the gap
avoid: Calling your experience irrelevant
A switch with no reason other than pay

items.prompt: Tell us about a time you worked under severe deadline pressure.
items.framing: Checks prioritisation, composure and execution, all of which matter in an intense MBA.
structure: Describe the situation and stakes
Explain how you prioritised and organised the work
Mention how you communicated with stakeholders
Describe the result and what you would do differently
avoid: Glorifying overwork without any learning
A vague story without specifics

items.prompt: Have you improved any process at work? Walk us through it.
items.framing: Looks for initiative and problem-solving. The panel likes candidates who spot inefficiency and fix it.
structure: Describe the process and the problem
Explain how you diagnosed it
Describe the change you proposed and how you got buy-in
State the effect and how you measured it
avoid: Inventing numbers
Taking sole credit for a team effort

items.prompt: Tell us about a difficult client or stakeholder you dealt with.
items.framing: Assesses empathy, communication and problem-solving with external parties.
structure: Set the context and what made the stakeholder difficult
Explain how you understood their real concern
Describe what you did to resolve the situation
Mention the outcome and the relationship afterwards
avoid: Mocking the client
A story without resolution

items.prompt: Have you faced an ethical dilemma at work? What did you do?
items.framing: Tests integrity and judgement. The panel wants to see how you reason through pressure.
structure: Describe the dilemma without naming people or confidential details
Explain the competing pressures
Describe what you did and why
Reflect on the consequences
avoid: Sharing confidential information
A story where you took no action

items.prompt: What is the most important thing your job has taught you?
items.framing: The panel looks for reflection - lessons about people, organisations and yourself.
structure: Name one lesson clearly
Illustrate it with a specific situation
Explain how it has changed your behaviour
avoid: Generic lessons like 'hard work pays off'
Listing many lessons superficially

items.prompt: Have you managed or mentored anyone? How did you go about it?
items.framing: Tests early people-management experience, even if informal.
structure: Describe the situation - an intern, a junior, a new joiner
Explain your approach: setting expectations, support, feedback
Describe the outcome for them and the team
Mention what you would do differently
avoid: Claiming large management responsibility you did not have
Describing only tasks you delegated

items.prompt: What is a recent development in your industry that excites you, and why?
items.framing: The panel wants to see whether you look beyond your daily tasks at the forces shaping your field, and whether you can connect a trend to business consequences. Genuine curiosity and the ability to explain impact matter more than picking a glamorous topic.
structure: Pick one development you have followed closely enough to explain in plain language - ideally one that touched your own work or team.
Describe what changed in two or three sentences, using only facts you have checked from reliable sources yourself.
Explain why it matters: who gains, who loses, and what it does to costs, customers or competition in your industry.
Give your own view on where it could go next and one risk or open question you are still unsure about.
Close by linking it to what you want to learn in an MBA or the role you are aiming for.
avoid: Choosing a buzzword topic you cannot explain beyond the headline.
Quoting figures you are not sure of - one wrong number invites a cross-examination.
Sounding excited without saying what the development actually changes.

items.prompt: Pick an economic policy debate and argue both sides for me.
items.framing: This tests balance, structured thinking and intellectual honesty. The panel checks whether you understand trade-offs rather than slogans, and whether you can hold a position after weighing the other side fairly.
structure: Name the debate and state the core trade-off in one line, for example growth versus fiscal discipline or consumer prices versus producer incomes.
Make the strongest case for the policy, with the mechanism by which it is supposed to work and who benefits.
Make the strongest case against it with equal seriousness - unintended effects, costs, implementation gaps.
State where you land and the condition under which you would change your mind.
Acknowledge any part of the evidence you have not studied deeply instead of improvising.
avoid: Arguing one side with conviction and treating the other side as a strawman.
Picking a debate you only know from social media headlines.
Refusing to take any position when asked for your own view.

items.prompt: How do you keep yourself updated on what is happening in the world?
items.framing: The panel is checking the quality of your information diet and whether your answer is real. They will often follow up with 'So what did you read this morning?', so the habit you describe must be one you actually practise.
structure: Describe your actual routine honestly - what you read or listen to, how often, and when in your day.
Show variety: a general news source, something specific to your field, and one source that gives a different perspective.
Explain how you verify things - cross-checking claims, preferring primary documents, being careful with forwarded messages.
Mention one thing you learnt recently through this habit and be ready to discuss it.
If your habit has gaps, say how you are improving it rather than overstating it.
avoid: Listing many sources you clearly do not follow.
Saying 'social media' as the main source without any filter for reliability.
Being unable to name a single item you read in the last few days.

items.prompt: What do you think of the state of startups in your home state?
items.framing: The panel wants to see whether you observe your surroundings with a business lens. They assess whether you can reason about ecosystems - talent, capital, infrastructure, policy, culture - using what you have seen first-hand, without inventing data.
structure: Start with what you have personally observed: types of ventures you know of, people around you starting businesses, sectors that seem active.
Organise your view using a simple frame such as talent, funding, market access, infrastructure and mindset.
Point out one strength and one bottleneck, with a concrete example from your own experience where possible.
Suggest one realistic improvement and who would need to act on it.
Be clear about the limits of your knowledge - say what you would want to verify before making a firm claim.
avoid: Throwing out numbers or rankings you cannot back up.
Speaking only about big-city ecosystems when asked about your home state.
Being dismissive or purely negative without suggesting any way forward.

items.prompt: I am going to ask you about a topic you may not know well. What do you do when you do not know the answer?
items.framing: Interviewers deliberately probe the edge of your knowledge. They are assessing honesty, composure and how you reason from first principles - not whether you know everything.
structure: Admit clearly and calmly what you do not know - one sentence is enough.
Share what you do know that is related, and reason aloud from basic principles about how the issue probably works.
Label your reasoning as an inference, not a fact.
Offer to read up on it and, if relevant, ask the panel a thoughtful question about it.
avoid: Bluffing - panels usually know the topic better and will push until the bluff collapses.
Freezing or apologising repeatedly instead of moving forward.
Saying 'I don't know' and stopping without any attempt to think aloud.

items.prompt: Which technology trend do you think will most change the way businesses work over the next decade?
items.framing: This tests whether you can think about technology in terms of business models, jobs and customers rather than hype. The panel values reasoning and nuance over predictions stated with false certainty.
structure: Choose a trend you understand at a working level, ideally one you have used or seen used.
Explain the mechanism - what task becomes cheaper, faster or possible that was not before.
Describe the business impact on one or two specific functions or industries.
Discuss the downsides and constraints: cost, skills, regulation, trust, or job displacement.
End with how you personally plan to build skills around it.
avoid: Using jargon without being able to explain it simply.
Making sweeping claims like 'it will replace all jobs' without reasoning.
Ignoring the risks and ethical questions entirely.

items.prompt: Tell me about a social or economic issue you care about deeply.
items.framing: The panel is looking for conviction backed by understanding, and for signs of empathy and maturity. They want to know if your concern goes beyond opinion into some understanding of causes and possible solutions.
structure: Name the issue and briefly explain why it matters to you - a personal connection makes it credible.
Describe the root causes as you understand them, separating what you have verified from what you believe.
Discuss one or two approaches to address it and the trade-offs each involves.
Mention anything you have done about it, however small, or what you would like to do.
Stay open to counter-arguments if the panel pushes back.
avoid: Choosing a topic only because it sounds impressive.
Delivering a rehearsed speech that cannot survive one follow-up question.
Taking an extreme or polarising stance and becoming defensive.

items.prompt: If you were asked about the most recent national budget, what would you focus on?
items.framing: Budget questions test whether you follow economic policy and can analyse priorities rather than recite announcements. The panel checks how you structure fiscal information and relate it to sectors or your own field.
structure: Before the interview, read the main themes from an official or reliable summary yourself, and note only points you are sure of.
In the answer, structure around a few lenses: spending priorities, revenue measures, and the fiscal position.
Pick one or two measures relevant to your background or target sector and explain their likely effect.
Give a balanced view - what you think works and what concerns you.
If you have not studied a part of it, say so and stick to what you know.
avoid: Reciting a list of announcements without any analysis.
Misquoting figures - if unsure, describe the direction rather than the number.
Discussing it purely in political terms instead of economic ones.

items.prompt: How does a major global development affect India? Pick one and explain.
items.framing: The panel checks whether you can connect global events to domestic consequences through clear economic links - trade, prices, capital flows, supply chains, geopolitics - and whether you reason carefully rather than repeat headlines.
structure: Choose a type of development you have followed and verified, for example a shift in trade policy, energy prices or supply chains.
Trace the transmission channels step by step: how does it reach Indian consumers, firms or the government?
Distinguish short-term effects from longer-term ones.
Identify which sectors or groups might gain and which might be hurt.
Offer a view on how India could respond, while noting what remains uncertain.
avoid: Picking a topic you only know at a headline level.
Describing the event at length without ever reaching its effect on India.
Claiming certainty about outcomes that even experts debate.

items.prompt: Should the government regulate more or less in a sector you know well?
items.framing: This assesses your understanding of the balance between market freedom and public interest. The panel wants nuance, an awareness of stakeholders, and grounding in your own sector experience.
structure: Pick a sector you have worked in or studied closely.
Explain what regulation is trying to achieve there - safety, fairness, competition, consumer protection.
Describe where it helps and where it may create friction, using examples from your experience.
Propose a balanced view, for example clearer rules with lighter compliance, and justify it.
Acknowledge what you would need to know more about before being definitive.
avoid: A simple 'less regulation is always better' or the opposite.
Criticising specific officials or institutions instead of discussing design.
Speaking about a sector you have no exposure to when a familiar one was available.

items.prompt: What was the most interesting thing you read in the news this week?
items.framing: The panel is checking whether you actually engage with news and can explain why something matters. Your choice also reveals your interests, so pick something you can discuss in depth.
structure: Pick an item you read fully and understood, preferably related to business, economy or your field.
Summarise it in a few sentences, sticking to facts you are confident about.
Explain why it caught your interest and what its implications could be.
Offer your own take and invite discussion by noting an open question.
avoid: Naming something you only saw as a headline.
Choosing a celebrity or entertainment story with no larger angle.
Adding details from memory that you are not sure are accurate.

items.prompt: Explain a basic economic concept like inflation or interest rates in a way your family would understand.
items.framing: This tests conceptual clarity and communication. Managers must explain complex ideas simply. The panel also checks whether you can connect concepts to everyday life without errors.
structure: Give a simple definition in one line using everyday language.
Use a relatable example from household life, such as grocery bills or a loan EMI.
Explain the cause-and-effect chain in two or three steps.
Mention why it matters to a business or the economy as a whole.
Check that your example is accurate - accuracy is better than cleverness.
avoid: Using textbook jargon that the 'family' would not understand.
Getting the direction of a relationship wrong, for example how rates affect borrowing.
Over-elaborating until the core idea is lost.

items.prompt: What are the biggest challenges facing the sector you want to work in after your MBA?
items.framing: The panel tests whether your career goal is researched and realistic. Knowing a sector's challenges shows that you have thought beyond its attractive surface.
structure: Name the sector and the role you are aiming for.
Lay out two or three challenges grouped logically, for example demand, cost, talent or regulation.
For each, explain briefly why it is a challenge and who it affects most.
Share how firms are trying to respond in general terms, and what you think could work.
Connect one challenge to a skill you hope to build during the MBA.
avoid: Only talking about the positives of the sector.
Naming challenges you cannot explain when asked 'why?'.
Using specific numbers or company claims you cannot verify.

items.prompt: How do you decide whether a piece of news is true?
items.framing: In an age of information overload, the panel wants to see critical thinking and source discipline - qualities essential for business decision-making.
structure: Describe your checks: who is the source, is there a primary document, do several independent outlets agree?
Mention how you treat forwarded messages, screenshots and anonymous claims.
Give an example of a time you avoided sharing or believing something that turned out to be wrong.
Connect this habit to decision-making in a workplace - verifying data before acting on it.
avoid: Claiming you never get misled - nobody is immune.
Naming a source as 'always reliable' without any reasoning.
Turning the answer into a political argument.

items.prompt: What do you see as one strength and one weakness of the Indian economy today?
items.framing: The panel checks for a balanced, informed perspective and the ability to structure big-picture thinking. Precision with claims and humility about complex issues both count.
structure: Pick one strength you can explain through a clear mechanism, for example a young workforce or a large domestic market.
Pick one weakness or challenge and explain why it constrains growth or wellbeing.
Avoid exact figures unless you have verified them; describe direction and scale qualitatively instead.
Suggest how the weakness could be addressed and who would need to act.
Acknowledge that reasonable people disagree on priorities.
avoid: Being purely celebratory or purely pessimistic.
Stringing together many points without explaining any of them.
Quoting statistics you are not certain of.

items.prompt: You mention reading as a hobby. What was the last book you read, and what did you disagree with in it?
items.framing: This checks whether the hobby is real and whether you read critically. The panel wants evidence of independent thought - engaging with an author's argument, not just summarising.
structure: Name the book and give a short, accurate summary of its main idea.
Say what you found valuable or convincing.
Identify one specific point you disagreed with or found weak, and explain why using reasoning or your own experience.
Mention how the book changed or confirmed your thinking in some way.
avoid: Naming a book you have not actually finished or cannot discuss in detail.
Saying you agreed with everything - it suggests passive reading.
Listing a popular self-help title without any reflection.

items.prompt: You play a team sport. What has it taught you that is useful for management?
items.framing: The panel wants concrete transferable lessons, not cliches. They look for specific moments that shaped how you handle teamwork, pressure, losing and leadership.
structure: Name the sport and your level or role honestly.
Describe one specific episode - a match, a losing streak, a team conflict - and what you did.
Draw out one or two lessons, for example playing to team strengths or recovering from setbacks.
Connect each lesson to a workplace or team situation you have faced or expect to face.
avoid: Generic lines like 'it taught me teamwork' with no story.
Exaggerating your level of play - follow-up questions will expose it.
Listing many lessons without depth on any.

items.prompt: You have listed music as a hobby. Tell me about how you practise and what keeps you going.
items.framing: This checks authenticity, discipline and self-motivation. Long-term hobbies reveal how you build skill over time without external pressure.
structure: Describe what you play, sing or listen to, and how long you have been at it.
Explain your practice routine honestly - frequency, how you learn, how you measure progress.
Share a challenge you faced, such as a plateau or performance nerves, and how you worked through it.
Reflect on what this discipline says about how you approach learning in general.
avoid: Claiming a level of expertise you cannot demonstrate if asked.
Being unable to answer basic questions about your own hobby.
Describing music only as relaxation when the panel asks about effort.

items.prompt: Tell me about your volunteering experience. What impact did you actually make?
items.framing: The panel probes whether the volunteering was meaningful or token. They value honest reflection about impact, what you learnt from the people you served, and whether you stayed committed.
structure: Describe the organisation or cause and your specific role.
Explain what you did concretely and for how long.
Be honest about impact - describe outcomes you saw without inflating them.
Share what you learnt about people, constraints or yourself.
Mention whether you are still involved, or why not.
avoid: Presenting a one-day event as a long commitment.
Talking about the beneficiaries in a patronising way.
Claiming large impact you cannot describe concretely.

items.prompt: You held a position of responsibility in college. What did you change that would not have happened without you?
items.framing: This tests real leadership versus titles. The panel wants a specific initiative, your role in driving it, how you handled people, and the result.
structure: Name the role and its scope briefly.
Describe the problem or opportunity you saw.
Explain the actions you personally took, including persuading others or handling resistance.
State the outcome honestly and what you would do differently.
Give credit to the team where due while making your contribution clear.
avoid: Listing duties of the post instead of a specific contribution.
Taking credit for everything the team did.
Choosing an example with no measurable or observable outcome.

items.prompt: You have listed a hobby here, but it seems you have not practised it lately. Is it really your hobby?
items.framing: The panel tests honesty and self-awareness. Many candidates list hobbies they have drifted away from; the panel respects candour and is wary of defensiveness.
structure: Acknowledge honestly if you have not practised it recently.
Explain briefly why - work, exams, relocation - without making excuses.
Show the hobby still matters: what you did in the past and what you still do in small ways.
Share a realistic plan to get back to it, or say what has replaced it.
avoid: Insisting you practise it regularly when you do not.
Getting defensive or blaming circumstances at length.
Being unable to discuss even basics of the hobby.

items.prompt: What has your hobby taught you about management?
items.framing: The panel wants to see reflective thinking - can you extract principles from everyday activities? Specific, honest links score higher than forced analogies.
structure: Pick one hobby and one clear lesson rather than many.
Tell a short story from the hobby that illustrates the lesson.
Translate it into a management principle, such as planning under uncertainty or managing resources.
Give an example of where you applied it outside the hobby.
avoid: Forcing an analogy that does not hold up.
Cliches without a real example.
Talking for too long about the hobby and too little about the lesson.

items.prompt: You enjoy travelling. What did a trip teach you about people or business?
items.framing: Travel is a common hobby; the panel looks for observation and curiosity beyond sightseeing. They want to see whether you notice how places, people and economies work.
structure: Describe one trip briefly and something specific you observed - a local business, a cultural practice, a problem.
Explain what that observation made you think about.
Connect it to a broader insight about customers, markets or people.
Show how it has shaped your outlook or decisions.
avoid: Listing destinations like a travel log.
Making sweeping generalisations about a community or region.
Having no real reflection beyond 'it was beautiful'.

items.prompt: You list fitness and running. How do you stay consistent, and what happens when you miss your goals?
items.framing: This tests discipline, goal-setting and how you handle setbacks - traits that predict how you will handle a demanding MBA.
structure: Describe your routine and the goals you set.
Explain the systems that keep you consistent, such as tracking, a partner or fixed timings.
Share an honest instance where you fell short and how you responded.
Link the habit to how you manage other commitments.
avoid: Claiming you never miss a day.
Focusing only on achievements without the process.
Exaggerating distances or results you cannot back up.

items.prompt: Cooking is an unusual hobby to list. What does it say about you?
items.framing: Unusual hobbies invite curiosity; the panel tests whether you can explain your interest with depth and connect it to traits like experimentation, planning or patience.
structure: Explain how you got into it and what you enjoy cooking.
Share a specific experiment or failure and what you learnt.
Draw out a trait it shows, such as planning, improvising with constraints or feeding a group on a budget.
Be ready for a quick practical question about something you cook.
avoid: Being apologetic about the hobby.
Overreaching with grand management analogies.
Being unable to answer simple questions about your own dishes.

items.prompt: You were active in quizzing or debating. Debate me now: argue the side you personally disagree with.
items.framing: The panel tests whether the skill is real, and also your flexibility of thought and composure. Arguing against your own view shows intellectual maturity.
structure: Accept the challenge calmly and briefly state your actual position first.
Make the opposing case with two or three genuine, well-reasoned points.
Present them fairly and persuasively without mocking them.
Conclude by noting what the exercise taught you or where the opposing side has a fair point.
avoid: Refusing or arguing weakly to signal your real view.
Making it personal or emotional.
Rambling without structure despite claiming debating skills.

items.prompt: You paint or write creatively. How does creativity fit into a business career?
items.framing: The panel wants to see whether you value creativity beyond the hobby itself, and whether you can relate it to problem-solving, communication or design thinking.
structure: Describe your creative practice briefly and honestly.
Explain what the creative process involves for you - ideation, iteration, feedback.
Connect that process to business tasks such as product design, marketing or solving open-ended problems.
Give an example from work or college where creative thinking helped.
avoid: Treating creativity and business as completely opposed.
Overclaiming the commercial value of your hobby.
Being vague about what you actually create.

items.prompt: Tell me about an event you organised. What went wrong, and how did you handle it?
items.framing: Event organising reveals planning, coordination and crisis management. The panel is more interested in how you handled the problem than in the event's scale.
structure: Describe the event and your role in a sentence or two.
Explain what went wrong and why.
Describe the immediate action you took and how you coordinated others.
Share the outcome and what process you changed afterwards.
avoid: Claiming nothing went wrong.
Blaming others for the problem.
Spending most of the time describing the event instead of the problem.

items.prompt: You list gaming as a hobby. Isn't that a waste of time?
items.framing: A mild stress angle on a hobby that panels sometimes view sceptically. They test whether you can defend your choices maturely, with balance and self-awareness.
structure: Stay calm and acknowledge the concern is reasonable when gaming is excessive.
Explain how you game and how much - with moderation that is honest.
Draw out genuine skills or interests it builds, such as strategy, team coordination or interest in game design.
Show you balance it with other commitments.
avoid: Getting defensive or dismissive of the question.
Overstating its benefits.
Admitting it takes up excessive time without any reflection.

items.prompt: You do not seem to have strong hobbies. What do you do outside work or studies?
items.framing: The panel wants to know you as a person and to see whether you have interests that recharge you. Honesty and genuine curiosity count more than impressive activities.
structure: Answer honestly about how you spend free time, even if it is simple.
Pick one activity and describe why you enjoy it and what you get from it.
Show curiosity - something you are exploring or learning on your own.
If you want to build a new interest, say what and why, without overselling it.
avoid: Inventing a hobby on the spot.
Saying you have no time for anything outside work.
Giving a long list with no depth.

items.prompt: Teach me something about your hobby in one minute.
items.framing: This tests communication, structure and genuine depth in the hobby. Explaining simply under time pressure is a core managerial skill.
structure: Choose one small, specific concept rather than the whole hobby.
Start with why it matters, then explain it in two or three simple steps.
Use an analogy or quick example the panel can relate to.
Close by checking understanding or offering a one-line summary.
avoid: Trying to cover too much in one minute.
Using jargon from the hobby without explaining it.
Running well over time.

items.prompt: A teammate presents your work as their own in a meeting with senior management. What do you do?
items.framing: The panel assesses emotional control, assertiveness and professional maturity. They want to see you protect your contribution without damaging the team or creating a public scene.
structure: Stay composed in the meeting; if natural, add to the discussion in a way that shows your understanding of the work.
Speak to the teammate privately afterwards - assume it may be a misunderstanding and state the facts calmly.
Agree how credit will be shared going forward, and keep records of your contributions.
If it repeats, raise it with your manager factually, focusing on the work rather than the person.
Reflect on whether your own communication about your work could be more visible.
avoid: Confronting the teammate in front of senior management.
Doing nothing and quietly resenting it.
Running to the manager before speaking to the person.

items.prompt: You see your close friend cheating in an important exam. What do you do?
items.framing: This tests integrity when loyalty pulls the other way. The panel looks for a clear ethical stance balanced with empathy and sensible action.
structure: Acknowledge the conflict between friendship and fairness openly.
State clearly that cheating is unfair to other students and that you would not cover for it.
Speak to your friend directly and promptly, urging them to come clean, and understand what pressure led to it.
If the situation is serious or continues, inform the appropriate authority, following the institution's process.
Explain how you would try to support your friend through the consequences.
avoid: Saying you would ignore it because they are your friend.
Publicly shaming them.
Giving a vague answer that never takes a position.

items.prompt: Your manager asks you to adjust some numbers in a report so the quarter looks better. How do you respond?
items.framing: A core ethics question. The panel wants a firm refusal to misrepresent data, combined with professional tact and knowledge of proper escalation routes.
structure: Clarify first - ask exactly what is being requested, in case it is a legitimate reclassification you misunderstood.
If it is misrepresentation, decline politely but clearly, explaining the risks to the company and to both of you.
Offer a constructive alternative: present accurate numbers with context, explanations and a recovery plan.
If pressure continues, escalate through proper channels such as a senior leader, compliance or the ethics function.
Keep written records of the request and your response.
avoid: Agreeing because 'everyone does it' or to protect your job.
Leaking the matter outside the company before using internal channels.
Refusing rudely without offering any alternative.

items.prompt: A client offers you an expensive gift after you closed a deal with them. What do you do?
items.framing: The panel checks your understanding of conflicts of interest and company policy, and whether you can handle the moment without offending the client.
structure: Thank the client warmly for the gesture.
Check and follow your organisation's gifts policy; when in doubt, consult your manager or compliance.
If it exceeds the policy, decline politely, explaining it is a company rule, or declare and hand it over as required.
Keep the relationship strong through professional means and good service.
avoid: Accepting quietly because the deal is already closed.
Declining in a way that embarrasses the client.
Assuming no policy applies without checking.

items.prompt: You have one promotion slot and two equally deserving team members. How do you decide?
